strengths: Addresses a practically important and challenging task: synthesizing immersive, free-flight navigable 3D urban scenes from multi-view satellite imagery, with applications in simulation, gaming, and robotics.

Proposes a complete two-stage pipeline with several tailored components: appearance modeling for multi-date satellite images, entropy-based opacity regularization, pseudo-camera depth supervision, curriculum-based iterative dataset update, and multi-sample diffusion refinement to improve cross-view consistency.

Provides extensive experimental validation on two datasets (DFC2019 and GoogleEarth), comparing against satellite reconstruction and city-generation baselines, with per-AOI results, ablations, user studies, and rendering-efficiency measurements. The reported improvements in FID/CMMD and user preference are substantial.

The paper is clearly written, includes detailed implementation and dataset information, discusses limitations, and provides reproducibility, ethics, and LLM-usage statements. Code release is promised.
Demonstrates real-time rendering after optimization (11 FPS on T4, 40 FPS on MacBook Air M2), which supports the claimed immersive exploration use case.
weaknesses: The core novelty is largely incremental: the method integrates existing 3D Gaussian Splatting, WildGaussians-style appearance modeling, FlowEdit-based diffusion editing, and iterative dataset update/curriculum learning. The main advance is system-level adaptation to satellite imagery rather than a fundamentally new algorithm.

Evaluation relies on Google Earth Studio renders as reference/ground truth, which is a synthetic proxy and may not fully validate true geometric accuracy. Because diffusion refinement can hallucinate plausible but incorrect facades, the metrics may reward GES-like appearance over physically correct 3D structure.

The depth supervision loss in Eq. (3) is written as minimizing the absolute Pearson correlation, which appears contradictory to the goal of aligning rendered and estimated depths. The formulation should be corrected or clarified; reliance on monocular depth (MoGe) also introduces scale ambiguity and potential bias.

Comparison with CityDreamer and GaussianCity may not be entirely apples-to-apples: those methods require semantic maps/height fields and are trained on the GoogleEarth dataset, while the proposed method consumes satellite-like images. The paper should better clarify input settings, adaptations, and fairness of these comparisons.

The GoogleEarth experiments use Google Earth Studio renders at 80° elevation as inputs rather than real satellite imagery, so the claim of operating solely on satellite imagery is only partially validated across datasets.

Optimization is computationally expensive (approximately 1 hour for reconstruction plus 6 hours for synthesis per scene) and depends on a large pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model; scalability to larger urban areas and extreme street-level views remains limited, as acknowledged by the authors.

Some strong claims, such as being the 'first' method of this kind, may be overstated given prior satellite-to-3D and city-generation work; the paper would benefit from more precise framing of its specific technical contributions.

strengths: The problem is well motivated and practically relevant: satellite imagery is abundant, geo-referenced, and cheap, so building navigable 3D city scenes from it addresses a real bottleneck in 3D content creation.

The two-stage pipeline (initial 3DGS reconstruction from satellite views, followed by curriculum-based iterative dataset update with a T2I diffusion prior) is a sensible engineering combination, and the paper thoughtfully adapts several existing ingredients (WildGaussians-style appearance embeddings, entropy opacity regularization, MoGe-based pseudo-camera depth supervision) to the satellite regime.

Evaluation is broad: two datasets (DFC2019, GoogleEarth), comparisons against both reconstruction (Sat-NeRF, EOGS, Mip-Splatting, CoR-GS) and city-generation (CityDreamer, GaussianCity) baselines, per-AOI tables, user studies with ~89 participants, ablations on both stages, and a rendering-efficiency analysis.
Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: implementation details, hyperparameters, camera sampling strategy, and dataset coordinates are documented, and code/data release is promised.
Limitations (compute cost, over-smoothed extreme street-level views, lack of robust geometric validation) are explicitly stated rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The central scientific claim is not adequately supported. The satellite input cannot observe building facades, so the "reconstructed" ground-level content is hallucinated by the diffusion prior. The paper repeatedly claims "satellite-to-ground 3D consistency" and "geometric accuracy," but there is no ground-truth ground-level data to verify that hallucinated facades are correct. "Consistency" here reduces to perceptual plausibility, not geometric fidelity, and the framing overstates what is demonstrated.

Evaluation is potentially circular on the GoogleEarth split. The method's training inputs (rendered at 80° elevation) and the reference frames (rendered at 17°/45° from GES) both come from the same Google Earth Studio 3D asset that also trained CityDreamer/GaussianCity. Reporting large PSNR/SSIM gains against GES renders does not establish real-world correctness, and distribution metrics such as FID_CLIP and CMMD are known to reward natural-image appearance, which a strong T2I prior trivially provides. The dramatic FID_CLIP improvements (e.g., 88 → 27) are therefore not convincing evidence of better geometry.

Novelty is limited relative to the claims. The core refinement mechanism is essentially the Iterative Dataset Update scheme of Instruct-NeRF2NeRF/IM-3D combined with FlowEdit, and the remaining components (opacity entropy regularization, per-image/per-Gaussian appearance embeddings, monocular depth supervision) are established techniques adapted from prior work. The "first" and "without costly 3D annotations / no domain-specific training" claims are therefore overstated, especially since the method depends heavily on large pretrained natural-image diffusion models.

Several key baseline comparisons are missing because the authors state the code/models are unavailable (Sat2Scene, Sat2Vid, EO-NeRF, Sat-DN, SatelliteRF, Sat-Mesh, CrossViewDiff, SkySplat), which weakens the claim of outperforming "state of the art" in satellite-to-scene synthesis.

The curriculum ablation is weak evidence for the proposed contribution: random view sampling (34.11/3.19) already improves substantially over no curriculum (33.79/3.36), and the curriculum only modestly improves to 28.35/2.88, so the ordering effect is not cleanly isolated. The multi-sample diffusion contribution is likewise only demonstrated with a two-cell ablation.

Pixel-level metrics are presented on hallucinated regions (facades, ground) where no meaningful reference exists, so PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS numbers in Tables 1/2/8/9 largely measure agreement with GES renders rather than reconstruction accuracy. The claim that these metrics are "meaningful for the GoogleEarth dataset" does not resolve the circularity concern.

Computational cost is high (roughly 1 h reconstruction + 6 h synthesis per scene on an A6000) and scales poorly; the practical impact of the method for city-scale deployment is consequently uncertain, and the efficiency claims rely on favorable comparisons (e.g., CityDreamer on A100).

The over-smoothing at extreme street-level views and the inability to validate hallucinated geometry are acknowledged only briefly; given that the paper's headline application is immersive ground-level navigation, this is a substantial limitation rather than a minor caveat.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely valuable and under-served problem: synthesizing free-flight navigable 3D urban scenes from readily available multi-view satellite imagery, without any 3D/scene-level annotations. The motivation is well argued (coverage, cost, and resolution of satellite data vs. the difficulty of collecting city-scale 3D scans).
The paper is clearly written and well organized. The two-stage pipeline (reconstruction then synthesis) is easy to follow, and Figure 3 gives an effective overview of the method and its components.

The curriculum-based insight is concrete and empirically grounded: Figure 4 demonstrates that satellite-trained 3DGS renders degrade as elevation decreases, which directly motivates the descending-elevation Iterative Dataset Update. This is the most original element of the paper and is validated in the ablations (Table 4, Figure 8c-d).

The reconstruction stage is carefully engineered: RPC-to-perspective approximation via SatelliteSfM, WildGaussians-style per-image/per-Gaussian appearance modeling for multi-date imagery, entropy-based opacity regularization to suppress floaters, and scale-invariant (PCorr) pseudo-camera depth supervision. Each component is individually ablated (Table 3, Figure 8a-b) and shown to contribute.

The multiple-diffusion-samples idea (averaging several refined trajectories per view rather than committing to one denoising path) is a sensible, practically motivated remedy for cross-view inconsistency, and is supported by an ablation (Table 4).

The empirical evaluation is broad: two datasets (DFC2019 and GoogleEarth), four AOIs each, comparisons against satellite reconstruction methods (Sat-NeRF, EOGS, Mip-Splatting, CoR-GS) and city generation methods (CityDreamer, GaussianCity), plus user studies with 89 participants per comparison, and an efficiency analysis (11 FPS on T4, ~40 FPS on a MacBook Air M2).

The paper is reasonably reproducible: implementation details, loss weights, sampling strategy, prompts, dataset coordinates, and training images are provided in the appendix, and a code/dataset release is promised. The limitations section honestly notes over-smoothing at extreme street-level views and high computational cost.

The practical impact is credible: the method produces real-time-renderable 3DGS scenes from publicly available satellite data, which is attractive for simulation, entertainment, and robotics use cases.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely compositional. The pipeline assembles existing components — 3DGS (Kerbl et al.), WildGaussians-style appearance embeddings, entropy opacity regularization, monocular-depth supervision, Instruct-NeRF2NeRF/IM-3D-style iterative dataset update, and FlowEdit prompt-to-prompt editing. The genuinely new pieces are the descending-elevation curriculum and multi-sample diffusion averaging. This is a meaningful but modest algorithmic contribution, and the paper would benefit from a sharper articulation of what is technically new beyond the schedule design.

The repeated "first" claim (first city-block-scale 3D scene creation framework without costly 3D annotations; first method synthesizing immersive free-flight navigable 3D urban scenes from satellite imagery alone) is not adequately substantiated. Sat2Scene (Li et al., CVPR 2024), which generates 3D urban scenes from satellite images with diffusion, is essentially only mentioned in a footnote as lacking available code, and is not discussed or compared in the related work or experiments. Sat2Density, GeoDiffusion, Sat2Vid, and CrossViewDiff are also relegated to a footnote. The distinction from these closest works needs to be argued explicitly, not just asserted.

The paper claims "3D-justified geometry" and reports "geometric accuracy," but there is no quantitative geometric evaluation. FID_CLIP/CMMD are distribution/perceptual metrics that reward realistic appearance and would not penalize plausible-but-wrong hallucinated façades; PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS against GES renders are confounded by differing acquisition conditions (the authors themselves call them "secondary references"). No depth/DSM/LiDAR-based error, no multi-view consistency metric, and no measurement of whether hallucinated façade geometry matches the real structure. Given that the method's core selling point is geometry completion in occluded regions, this is a substantive gap.

The user study uses Google Earth Studio renders as the "ground truth" for the geometric-accuracy question. GES is itself a rendered 3D model of unverified accuracy, so "geometric accuracy" in the study is effectively a perceptual preference for GES-like appearance. This weakens the strongest empirical evidence offered for geometric fidelity.

Several design choices are heuristic and under-analyzed: the number of diffusion samples per view (Ns = 2), the number of episodes (Ne = 5), the elevation/radius schedules, and the FlowEdit prompt pairs and noise range (nmin=4, nmax=10) appear to be hand-tuned without sensitivity analysis. The theoretical justification for multi-sample diffusion ("the denoising trajectory distribution is a super-set of the optimal trajectories") is informal and not developed rigorously.

Comparisons with CityDreamer and GaussianCity are not strictly like-for-like, since those methods consume semantic maps and height fields rather than satellite imagery, and are evaluated on their own training distribution. The authors acknowledge this, but it means the head-to-head numbers should be interpreted cautiously.

The synthesis stage requires roughly 6 hours on an A6000 plus the reconstruction hour, and the method depends on a large external diffusion model (FLUX.1-dev) with manually engineered prompts. Prompt sensitivity and failure modes (e.g., plausible but incorrect structure insertion) are not analyzed, and the hallucination risk is only briefly acknowledged.

The reliance on MoGe monocular depth for pseudo-camera supervision introduces a scale-invariant, potentially inconsistent prior; the paper does not quantify how sensitive the reconstruction is to depth-estimator errors, nor does it validate the induced geometry against an independent source.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and challenging problem: synthesizing large-scale, navigable 3D urban scenes directly from multi-view satellite imagery, which has clear value for simulation, virtual navigation, robotics, and content creation.

The system design is well motivated and thoroughly integrated, combining 3D Gaussian Splatting with appearance modeling for multi-date satellite variability, opacity regularization, pseudo-depth supervision, and a curriculum-based iterative dataset update using a pre-trained diffusion editor.

Experiments are extensive: two datasets (DFC2019 and GoogleEarth), multiple reconstruction and city-generation baselines, ablations on both reconstruction and synthesis stages, user studies, multi-block scalability analysis, prompt sensitivity, and qualitative results.

The method achieves strong quantitative results on FID_CLIP and CMMD, competitive pixel-level metrics, and winning user-study preferences, while also demonstrating real-time rendering after appearance fusion (reported 60 FPS on consumer hardware).
The paper is well organized and clearly written, with helpful figures and a detailed supplementary material covering implementation, dataset splits, additional experiments, and resource analysis.
Practical limitations are acknowledged, including dependence on off-nadir satellite views, heuristic camera trajectory design, and the difficulty of purely nadir facade synthesis.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is largely integrative: the main components draw heavily on existing ideas such as WildGaussians-style appearance modeling, Mip-Splatting, entropy-based opacity regularization, MoGe depth supervision, Instruct-NeRF2NeRF/LucidDreamer-style iterative dataset updates, and FlowEdit diffusion refinement. The new contribution is their composition for satellite-to-urban 3D synthesis, which may be viewed as incremental for ECCV.

The claim of being the first method to synthesize this setting is somewhat overstated given concurrent works cited in the paper (e.g., Sat2Scene, Sat2RealCity, Sat3DGen, MagicCity), several of which are not empirically compared due to unavailable code or models, leaving the positioning incomplete.

The use of GoogleEarth Studio renders at 80° elevation as proxy satellite input is not equivalent to real multi-view satellite imagery, and comparing against CityDreamer and GaussianCity on their training dataset may not be a fully fair test of satellite-conditioned synthesis.

The diffusion refinement can hallucinate appearance details not grounded in the input satellite evidence. While prompt-to-prompt editing, multiple diffusion samples, and mixing refined/original views mitigate inconsistency, the paper provides no explicit 3D-consistency guarantee, and FID/CMMD against GES references may reward generative realism rather than satellite faithfulness.

Quantitative results are reported as single point estimates without variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and key user-study details are placed in the supplementary material, limiting direct assessment of robustness and statistical reliability in the main paper.

The method still requires off-nadir satellite views for facade synthesis, and the fixed heuristic camera trajectory can leave blind spots in complex geometries; these are acknowledged but remain substantive limitations for broad deployment.

strengths: The paper addresses a valuable and challenging problem: synthesizing immersive, navigable 3D urban scenes directly from satellite imagery, with potential applications in simulation, robotics, and virtual exploration.

The proposed two-stage pipeline is well motivated: it combines 3D Gaussian Splatting for geometric reconstruction with diffusion-based appearance refinement, and the curriculum-based IDU schedule from high to low elevation is intuitive and empirically supported by ablations.

The method includes several practical components for satellite imagery: multi-date appearance embeddings, entropy-based opacity regularization, pseudo-camera depth supervision, and multiple diffusion samples per view.
The system supports real-time rendering after fusing appearance embeddings into a standard 3DGS representation, with reported rendering speeds and scalability analysis.
The experimental section is extensive, covering DFC2019 and GoogleEarth datasets, multiple baselines, per-scene metrics, user studies, ablation studies, and supplementary qualitative results.
The supplementary material provides useful implementation details, additional qualitative comparisons, prompt sensitivity analysis, and multi-block scalability results.
Limitations are discussed, including reliance on off-nadir views and heuristic camera trajectories.
weaknesses: The evaluation on the GoogleEarth dataset is not convincing for a satellite-to-3D claim: the training inputs are Google Earth Studio renders at 80° elevation, not real satellite imagery, and the evaluation references are also GES renders. This creates a source-matched setup that cannot substantiate real satellite-to-ground generalization.

For DFC2019, the reference frames are GES renders with acknowledged illumination and color gaps. The reported pixel-level scores are extremely low (e.g., PSNR around 10–12, SSIM around 0.2–0.4, LPIPS high), and the main distribution metrics against GES do not objectively validate the correctness of hallucinated occluded regions such as building facades.

The core claim that synthesized facades remain consistent with satellite observations is not rigorously evaluated. There is no held-out satellite-view metric after diffusion refinement, so it is unclear whether FlowEdit introduces textures that conflict with the oblique satellite evidence.

The paper omits comparisons with many recent and directly relevant satellite-to-3D/city generation methods, such as Sat2Scene, Sat2City, Sat3DGen, MagicCity, Sat2RealCity, SkySplat, CityGaussian, and Horizon-GS. This is a significant omission given the paper’s first/SOTA claims.

Comparisons with CityDreamer and GaussianCity are not apples-to-apples: those methods use layout/height-map inputs, whereas Skyfall-GS uses satellite-like renderings. The paper does not fully disentangle whether gains come from the proposed refinement or from access to more image-like input.

The technical novelty is largely incremental: the method combines existing components (3DGS, WildGaussians-style appearance modeling, MoGe depth, FlowEdit/FLUX, Instruct-NeRF2NeRF-style IDU) with a heuristic curriculum over camera elevation. There is no fundamentally new algorithm or theoretical insight.

The multiple-diffusion-sample strategy lacks a rigorous justification. The argument that averaging over independently refined views approximates a 3D-consistent solution is informal, and no explicit cross-view consistency loss is introduced.
Ablations are mostly conducted on a single AOI, without error bars or multiple random seeds for the main results. Robustness and generalization claims are therefore under-supported.

The user study lacks important details: participant demographics, statistical significance, confidence intervals, and control for ordering or selection bias. The reported 80–94% win rates are therefore difficult to interpret.

Some methodological choices are under-justified: the PCorr depth loss ignores scale, MoGe is applied to rendered images in a potentially self-referential loop, and the effect of diffusion hallucination on geometric fidelity is not isolated.
The manuscript has presentation issues, including inconsistent table formatting, missing values in main tables, confusing section/algorithm numbering, and typos such as “Sat-ToRF” and “Splatting.”

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, the method depends heavily on large pretrained models (FLUX.1 dev, FlowEdit, MoGe), and training requires substantial compute (6–9 hours per block, up to 46 GB peak memory).

The claims are overstated in places: “first method” and “solely from satellite imagery” obscure reliance on large pretrained generative and depth models, and the demonstrated scale is block-level rather than truly city-wide.

strengths: Tackles an important and challenging problem: synthesizing explorable 3D urban scenes from multi-view satellite imagery without 3D or street-level training data, with practical applications in simulation, gaming, and robotics.

Proposes a well-motivated hybrid pipeline: 3D Gaussian Splatting with appearance modeling, opacity regularization, and pseudo-camera depth supervision, followed by curriculum-based Iterative Dataset Update using a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model for render refinement.

Provides extensive experiments on two datasets (DFC2019 and GoogleEarth), multiple baselines from satellite reconstruction and city generation, user studies, ablations, and supplementary analyses on complex geometries, bridges, prompt sensitivity, multi-block scalability, and transient objects.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed implementation settings, camera trajectories, prompts, dataset descriptions, and analysis of the RPC-to-perspective approximation.
Achieves real-time rendering after optimization and demonstrates a portable 3DGS representation compatible with standard renderers.
Acknowledges limitations such as fixed heuristic camera trajectories, artifacts at extreme street-level views, and the requirement for off-nadir satellite views.
weaknesses: Geometric fidelity in occluded regions is not robustly validated: main comparisons rely heavily on perceptual/distribution metrics such as FID_CLIP and CMMD plus user studies, while quantitative 3D geometry evaluation is limited to a coarse DSM ablation on one scene. The claim of '3D-justified geometry' therefore needs stronger support.

The diffusion refinement can hallucinate facade content inconsistent with the satellite observations, as even the supplementary stochastic diversity figure shows generated signage changing across samples. There is no quantitative metric ensuring semantic or geometric consistency of synthesized facades with the input satellite imagery.

Benchmark validity is limited: GoogleEarth evaluation uses synthetic Google Earth Studio renders and references rather than real satellite or street-level imagery, and DFC2019 references also come from GES rather than true ground-truth facades. Generalization to real-world satellite-to-street-level synthesis remains unproven.

Some closely related recent satellite-to-3D city generation methods, such as Sat2City and Sat2RealCity, are not compared because of unavailable code, even though they are relevant to the claimed setting; this weakens the empirical positioning of the contribution.

The immersive/free-flight/street-level navigation claim is somewhat overstated: the curriculum lowers elevation only to 45 degrees, and the limitations note severe artifacts at extreme street-level perspectives and the need for off-nadir satellite views. True ground-level navigation is not thoroughly demonstrated.

The method has substantial computational cost: roughly 6h45m per scene and 46GB peak GPU memory for a roughly 1km x 512m region. City-scale scalability remains expensive, and this limitation is not fully discussed.

Baseline fairness is not entirely clear: Mip-Splatting is augmented with the proposed appearance modeling on DFC2019, while other baselines are not similarly adapted, and some city generation baselines are trained on GoogleEarth and evaluated on GES renders, making cross-method comparisons less definitive.

The technical novelty is partly incremental: numerous individual components (3DGS, WildGaussians-style appearance modeling, entropy opacity regularization, monocular depth supervision, IDU with diffusion refinement) already exist; the main contribution is their integration and curriculum design for satellite imagery.
